title: Alberta: growth and public services
scopeNote: Published comparisons use different reporting periods. They show changes in demand, resources and access; they do not estimate how much any policy or migration caused those changes.
updatePolicy: Curated source snapshot, independently checked on the review date. Observation dates appear with each measure. Not a live feed.

sources.title: CIHI — Health System Context Series: Alberta
sources.note: Population profile updated July 2026. Population uses Statistics Canada tables 17-10-0005-01 and 17-10-0008-01, accessed April 2026. Hospital spending uses National Health Expenditure Trends 2025; 2025 is forecast. Capacity comparisons use Hospital Beds Staffed and In Operation 2023–2024.

sources.title: Statistics Canada — Public school enrolment and compensation, 2023/2024
sources.note: Financial figures in this release are inflation-adjusted to 2023/2024 dollars. Educators are reported counts, not a classroom-size measure.

sources.title: Financial Accountability Office of Ontario — Education Spending Plan Review, Figure 5.1
sources.note: School-board spending divided by students; FAO analysis of Statistics Canada tables 10-10-0019-01 and 37-10-0007-01. Canada comparison excludes New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and the territories; it includes Alberta.

sources.title: Alberta Health Services — Monitoring Measures, 2024–25 FQ4
sources.note: Provincial table, PDF page 2; fiscal fourth-quarter year-to-date columns. Data as of June 9, 2025. Emergency measure covers busiest sites; hip measure covers scheduled surgeries.

sources.title: CMHC — 2025 Rental Market Report
sources.note: October rental survey; census metropolitan areas. Turnover rent is rent paid by new tenants in two-bedroom purpose-built rental apartments, not average rent for every tenant.

sources.title: Alberta — K to 12 funding model
sources.note: Official enrolment weighting rules through 2024/25 and from 2025/26.

population.title: More people to serve
population.summary: Alberta grew faster than Canada. Population growth adds demand for services and can expand the workforce that delivers them.

metrics.label: Population growth
metrics.note: 2005 = 100. Uses CIHI’s published percentage changes; no annual path is inferred.

notes: CIHI reports Alberta’s population rounded to 3.3 million in 2005 and 5.0 million in 2025. The index uses the published 51.4% change, rather than recalculating from rounded counts.
Age and location also affect service needs. In 2025, Alberta’s median age was 38.1, compared with 40.6 nationally.

schools.title: School resources grew more slowly than enrolment
schools.summary: Student enrolment increased faster than educator numbers and inflation-adjusted instructional compensation.

metrics.label: Students, educators and compensation
metrics.note: 2022–23 = 100. Compensation covers salaries, wages and benefits for instructional and educational services staff, in constant 2023–24 dollars. It is not total school funding.

metrics.label: School-board spending per student
metrics.note: Canada average covers eight provinces, including Alberta. Excludes NB, NL and the territories. Current dollars; this spending comparison differs from inflation-adjusted compensation above.

notes: A lower spending rank does not establish an adequate funding level; provincial structures, costs and student needs differ.
The educator count is not class size and does not measure how staff are distributed between schools.

policy.text: Enrolment weighting changed from 20% previous, 30% current and 50% projected enrolment to 30% current and 70% projected enrolment. The school results above predate this change.

health.title: Capacity and access moved in different directions
health.period: Each measure has its own period
health.summary: Hospital spending per resident rose in nominal dollars. Acute beds per resident fell, while emergency waits and hip-surgery access moved in opposite directions.

metrics.label: Hospital spending per resident

series.label: Alberta
series.changeNote: CIHI published percentage; rounded dollar endpoints may yield a slightly different ratio.

series.label: Canada
series.changeNote: CIHI published percentage; rounded dollar endpoints may yield a slightly different ratio.

metrics.note: Current dollars, not inflation-adjusted. 2025 is a forecast. This covers provincial/territorial government hospital spending, not all health spending.

metrics.label: Acute hospital beds
metrics.note: 2014–15 = 100. Beds staffed and operating. Uses published changes (+4.2% count; −9.0% per-resident rate), not ratios of rounded bed counts.

metrics.label: Emergency stay before admission
metrics.note: Median emergency-department length of stay for admitted patients at busiest sites; lower is better. Full fiscal year-to-date comparisons.

metrics.label: Scheduled hip replacements within benchmark
metrics.note: Share of scheduled hip replacements completed within the CIHI benchmark; higher is better. Full fiscal year-to-date comparisons.

notes: These measures cover different services and periods. They cannot isolate effects of budgets, population change, staffing or care delivery.
Per-resident spending is not adjusted for age, patient complexity or local costs.

housing.title: Rental markets can move differently
housing.summary: New tenants paid less for a two-bedroom purpose-built apartment in Calgary, but more in Edmonton.

metrics.label: Two-bedroom rent for new tenants
metrics.note: Monthly turnover rents, current dollars. These are city-region survey averages, not every tenant’s bill or a province-wide rent index.

notes: Calgary’s purpose-built rental supply grew 11% in 2025; the vacancy rate was 5.0%.
CMHC describes both new supply and changing demand. This comparison does not identify a causal share for migration or government policy.
